title: Kubernetes Network Policies: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on controlling pod traffic with NetworkPolicies: the allow-all default, selectors, ingress and egress rules, default deny, DNS egress, CNI support, and testing.

chapters.title: Network Policies: What and Why
points: Default is allow-all: every pod can reach every other pod in any namespace, and no policy means no restriction
A NetworkPolicy is a namespaced allow-list firewall at L3/L4 (IP, port, protocol) applied to pods chosen by a selector
Policies are additive and allow-only: no deny rules, and if any policy selects a pod, traffic not matched by some policy is dropped for that direction
A pod is isolated for ingress or egress only once a policy selecting it lists that policyType; unselected pods stay open
Policies are stateful: reply traffic for an allowed connection is permitted automatically

chapters.title: Selectors and Rule Anatomy
points: spec.podSelector picks the pods the policy protects; an empty podSelector {} selects every pod in the policy's namespace
Rule peers in from/to: podSelector (same namespace), namespaceSelector (by namespace labels), ipBlock (CIDR with optional except)
namespaceSelector matches namespace labels, so label the namespace first (kubernetes.io/metadata.name is set automatically)
Example: ingress from podSelector app=frontend on ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 8080}] to pods app=api
Mistake: namespaceSelector and podSelector as two separate list items is OR, while both in one item is AND, and a missing dash flips the meaning

chapters.title: Ingress and Egress Rules
points: policyTypes: [Ingress] controls inbound to selected pods using from; [Egress] controls outbound using to; list both to control both
Ingress is evaluated at the destination pod and egress at the source pod, so a connection needs egress allowed at the source and ingress allowed at the destination
Omitting policyTypes defaults to Ingress, plus Egress only if the policy has an egress section
Multiple entries in from/to are ORed; the ports list restricts which ports apply to those peers; an omitted from/to with ports allows all peers on those ports
Mistake: allowing egress to a pod but forgetting ingress on the target (or vice versa) so traffic still drops

chapters.title: Default Deny and DNS Egress
points: Default deny ingress: podSelector {} with policyTypes [Ingress] and no ingress rules blocks all inbound to the namespace
Default deny egress: podSelector {} with policyTypes [Egress] and no egress rules blocks all outbound, including DNS
Default deny all: policyTypes [Ingress, Egress] with an empty podSelector; start here, then add allow policies per app
Allow DNS egress to kube-system pods k8s-app=kube-dns (namespaceSelector plus podSelector) on port 53 over both UDP and TCP
Mistake: denying egress without a DNS allow, so service names fail to resolve while direct IPs still work

chapters.title: CNI Support and Testing Policies
points: NetworkPolicy is enforced by the CNI plugin, not the API server: Calico, Cilium and Weave Net enforce it
Flannel alone does not enforce policies: the objects are accepted but silently ignored, giving false security
Test with a throwaway pod: kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -qO- --timeout=2 http://svc:8080
Test allowed and denied sources: run from a pod with the permitted label and from one without, in the right namespaces
Inspect with kubectl get netpol -n ns and kubectl describe netpol name to confirm selectors match the intended pods and labels

chapters.title: Network Policy Cheat Sheet
points: Defaults: no policy = allow all; any policy selecting a pod = allow only what is listed, per direction
Selectors: podSelector {} = all pods in the namespace; namespaceSelector needs namespace labels; ipBlock for CIDR with except
Same list item = AND, separate items = OR
Default deny all: podSelector {} + policyTypes [Ingress, Egress]
DNS allow: egress to kube-dns on UDP and TCP 53
Needs a policy-aware CNI (Calico or Cilium); verify with kubectl run busybox and wget --timeout
